--- title: "Trajectories and cases" --- The grid from [A scenario grid](scenario-grid.qmd) holds five campaigns run against one shared baseline. What comes back is five rows of scalars and five pairs of 157-step trajectories, and rebuilding it takes the same setting and the same five `Scenario` objects. ::: {#e6b6d80c .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from estimint import run_scenarios, preload_models from estimint.scenarios import Scenario, EirTarget setting = dict( res_use=0.30, Q0=0.85, phi=0.80, seasonal=0.0, irs=0.0, py_only=0.70, routine=0.0, eir_target=EirTarget(0.45, "prevalence"), ) grid = [ Scenario(name="Withdraw", **setting), Scenario(name="Pyrethroid-only", itn_future=0.70, net_type_future="pyrethroid_only", **setting), Scenario(name="PBO", itn_future=0.70, net_type_future="pyrethroid_pbo", **setting), Scenario(name="Pyrrole", itn_future=0.70, net_type_future="pyrethroid_pyrrole", **setting), Scenario(name="PBO + IRS + LSM", itn_future=0.70, net_type_future="pyrethroid_pbo", irs_future=0.60, lsm=0.30, **setting), ] res = run_scenarios(grid) ``` ::: The time grid comes off the emulator's own configuration rather than being hard-coded. ::: {#b7dd33a9 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} _, artifacts = preload_models() cfg = artifacts["prevalence"].preprocessing_config n_steps = cfg["n_steps"] window = cfg["window_size"] abs_t = cfg["model_start_day"] + window * np.arange(n_steps) years = (abs_t - cfg["intervention_day"]) / 365 idx_y9 = int(np.argmin(np.abs(abs_t - cfg["intervention_day"]))) idx_y9 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 78 ``` ::: ::: ## Prevalence trajectories ::: {#f6b02e04 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 4.0)) for _, row in res.iterrows(): ax.plot(years, np.asarray(row["prevalence"]), lw=1.8, label=row["name"]) ax.axvline(0, color="#8b93a3", ls="--", lw=1, alpha=0.7) ax.set_ylim(0, None) ax.set_ylabel("Prevalence (under 5)") ax.set_xlabel("Years since campaign") ax.legend(ncol=2, fontsize=8) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Under-five prevalence under five campaigns run against one baseline, from three years before the campaign to three years after. The dashed line marks the campaign.](comparing_files/figure-html/cell-5-output-1.png){fig-alt='Line chart of under-five prevalence for five scenarios sharing an x-axis in years since the campaign. All five overlap before the campaign at around 0.45. Afterwards the withdrawal scenario climbs to about 0.50, the three net scenarios dip and rebound to between 0.46 and 0.48, and the combination scenario falls below 0.05 and stays there.'} ::: ::: The five lines coincide to the left of the dashed line. That is the shared run-up under the pyrethroid-only nets already in place. After the campaign the three net scenarios reduce prevalence, reach a minimum roughly a year in, and converge towards one another as their insecticide decays, while withdrawal rises throughout and the combination scenario falls well below the other four and stays there. This is because IRS and larval source management do not decay on the same three-year clock a net does. The three net scenarios end the horizon within about two prevalence points of each other. At their minimum they were separated by considerably more. ## Clinical cases The same five scenarios carry a second trajectory, clinical incidence, on the emulator's own scale. ::: {#0ccaa1d4 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 4.0)) for _, row in res.iterrows(): ax.plot(years, np.asarray(row["cases"]), lw=1.8, label=row["name"]) ax.axvline(0, color="#8b93a3", ls="--", lw=1, alpha=0.7) ax.set_ylim(0, None) ax.set_ylabel("Clinical incidence") ax.set_xlabel("Years since campaign") ax.legend(ncol=2, fontsize=8) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Clinical incidence under the same five campaigns. The series oscillates from one 14-day window to the next.](comparing_files/figure-html/cell-6-output-1.png){fig-alt='Line chart of clinical incidence for the same five scenarios. The ordering follows the prevalence panel, but the series oscillates sharply from window to window, and by the right-hand edge the three net scenarios have converged into a band that overlaps withdrawal.'} ::: ::: Incidence oscillates from one 14-day window to the next, far more than prevalence does, and by the right-hand edge the three net scenarios have converged into a band that overlaps withdrawal. This is because prevalence measures existing infection, while incidence records new episodes per window. Incidence inherits the window's sampling noise. ::: {#19a93317 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} res[["name", "cases_endline"]].sort_values("cases_endline").round(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}
name cases_endline
4 PBO + IRS + LSM 0.1653
0 Withdraw 2.1272
3 Pyrrole 2.3899
2 PBO 2.4124
1 Pyrethroid-only 2.4331
``` ::: ::: Sorted on `cases_endline` alone, withdrawing the nets comes out ahead of every net scenario, an artefact of the column rather than something the campaigns did. The window is noisy, as the panel above shows. Clinical incidence is also not a monotone function of transmission, and the withdrawal scenario has spent three years at higher prevalence, so the simulator's immunity dynamics carry that through into fewer clinical episodes per person late in the horizon. ::: {.callout-note} ## A note on endline columns `prev_endline` and `cases_endline` are single 14-day windows. They are cheap to sort on and they throw away the three years over which a campaign does its work. Integrate the trajectory instead. ::: ## Cases averted Integrate `cases` from `idx_y9`, with the timestep expressed in years. ::: {#ae1fb22c .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} step_years = window / 365 burden = pd.Series( { row["name"]: float(np.trapezoid(np.asarray(row["cases"])[idx_y9:], dx=step_years)) for _, row in res.iterrows() }, name="burden", ) burden.round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` Withdraw 7.577 Pyrethroid-only 5.619 PBO 4.815 Pyrrole 4.548 PBO + IRS + LSM 0.295 Name: burden, dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: `cases` is reported on the emulator's own incidence scale, and because every scenario shares that scale, differences and percentages between them are meaningful without pinning the units. Taking withdrawal as the counterfactual gives the burden each campaign averts. ::: {#f68718a3 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} baseline = burden["Withdraw"] averted = ( pd.DataFrame( { "burden": burden, "averted": baseline - burden, "averted_pct": 100 * (baseline - burden) / baseline, } ) .sort_values("averted", ascending=False) .rename_axis("campaign") ) averted.round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ```{=html}
burden averted averted_pct
campaign
PBO + IRS + LSM 0.29 7.28 96.11
Pyrrole 4.55 3.03 39.98
PBO 4.81 2.76 36.46
Pyrethroid-only 5.62 1.96 25.85
Withdraw 7.58 0.00 0.00
``` ::: ::: ::: {#0aa31428 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} bars = averted.drop(index="Withdraw").sort_values("averted_pct") fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 3.4)) ax.barh(bars.index, bars["averted_pct"], height=0.55) ax.set_axisbelow(True) ax.set_xlabel("Clinical burden averted vs withdrawal (%)") ax.set_xlim(0, 100) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Clinical burden averted relative to withdrawing the nets, integrated over the three years after the campaign.](comparing_files/figure-html/cell-10-output-1.png){fig-alt='Horizontal bar chart of percentage of clinical burden averted relative to net withdrawal. The combination scenario averts about 96 per cent, pyrrole about 40 per cent, PBO about 36 per cent, and pyrethroid-only about 26 per cent.'} ::: ::: Integrated over the three years the nets are in the field, the three net scenarios are separated by around fourteen percentage points of averted burden. At endline they were separated by two prevalence points. The ordering of the net scenarios follows `dn0_future` and nothing else, so it is only as good as the resistance level supplied, and at a resistance of 0.30 the pyrethroid-only and the pyrrole net are far apart, while at 0.0 they are much closer. A resistance estimate carries error. Re-run the grid across its plausible range to see how much of the ordering survives it. ## See also [Exporting results](exporting.qmd) gets these tables and trajectories out of Python. [Nets and dn0](../04-estimint/nets-and-dn0.qmd) covers the resistance curves that set the ordering of the net scenarios. [EIR, HBR, prevalence, and cases](../03-concepts/equilibrium.qmd) covers why clinical incidence is not monotone in transmission.
